column3: It is the exact same formula: denying what God gave, temporary enjoyment, then coming knowledge.
Blessed rain and harvest do not clarify ingratitude, association, or the temporary reprieve in the focus.
Its brief worldly enjoyment followed by Hell closely supports the focus's warning that present enjoyment is not lasting security.
It nearly exactly repeats the focus, adding that the response follows rescue and safety granted by God.
Human-caused corruption and tasted consequence broadly complement the focus's warning of eventual consequences.
It identifies favor as from God, offering limited background for the focus's warning against denying the giver.
Its challenge to continue acting followed by "you will know" closely parallels the focus's deferred warning.
It directly names God as creator, provider, giver of death and life, then denies that alleged partners do any of these things.
Its mention of unbelief concerns neglect of alms and the Hereafter, not the focus's response to received blessing.
It explains the focus's "you will know" formula as disclosure of humiliating, lasting punishment.
Generic disobedience and unbelief do not specifically address blessing, association, or reprieve.
Divine testimony to revelation does not clarify the focus's warning about denying granted mercy.
It uses the same future-knowledge warning and locates it in the eventual outcome of wrongdoers.
The immediately preceding verse states the pattern the focus explains: people call on God in hardship, then associate partners after receiving mercy.
Provision for people and livestock shares only the general idea of enjoyment from God's provision.
It explicitly calls known material support God's continuing provision, supporting the focus's account of gifts whose source is denied.
It contrasts believers' recompense from divine bounty with God's dislike of unbelief, but does not develop the focus's warning.
It makes security and authority conditional on worship without association, and condemns unbelief after that blessing.
The righteous enjoy what their Lord gives them, a positive counterpart to the focus's misuse of divine gifts.
Reverence before the Messenger does not illuminate the focus's themes.
Its statement that only the knowledgeable grasp parables loosely supports the focus's call to recognize a moral truth.
Belief or denial of revealed signs only broadly parallels accepting or denying what God grants.
The immediate continuation challenges the associators to produce any authority speaking for their association.
It closely restates the pattern of calling on God in hardship, forgetting after a gift, making rivals, and being told to enjoy unbelief briefly.
Proper recitation of scripture and disbelief in it do not clarify the focus's specific argument.
Its diagnosis of knowledge limited to worldly life supports the focus's warning that present enjoyment obscures the coming reality.
The command not to exalt oneself over God does not establish a useful connection to the focus.
It joins worship of God alone with an explicit refusal to associate anything with Him.
Following the Messenger as proof of love for God does not clarify the focus's warning.
The command to enjoy until an appointed time directly frames enjoyment as a limited reprieve before judgment.
Earlier peoples' rejection of their messengers is only a general parallel to the focus's unbelief.
Its immediate context shows people exulting in mercy and despairing at harm, extending the focus's critique of their response to divine favor.
A warning of punishment before the final punishment loosely supports the focus's future consequence.
Provision described as enjoyment is only a limited lexical and thematic parallel.
The surrounding call to praise God provides a broad opposite response to the focus's ingratitude.
God's clarifying guidance before judging a people does not directly bear on the focus.
The regulation of prayer during danger does not clarify the focus's themes.
Testing believers to disclose endurance has no material connection to the focus.
It explicitly calls worldly enjoyment temporary, followed by return and severe punishment for disbelief.
It combines their disbelief in the reminder with the exact warning that they will come to know.
The nearby verse identifies expanding and restricting provision as God's sign, supporting the focus's emphasis on the true giver.
God's knowledge of concealed and public speech does not clarify this warning about granted blessing.
It closely matches the focus by joining eating, enjoyment, distracting hope, and the warning that they will know.
The surah's closing assurance that God's promise is true broadly supports the certainty of the focus's future warning.
The description of desert Arabs' distance from revealed limits does not clarify the focus.
It preserves the same deferred "they will know" warning after the Messenger withdraws from futile dispute.
It presents a grateful use of provision, eating while naming God and feeding the poor, as a loose positive contrast.
The Companions' careful purchase of food does not illuminate the focus's themes.
It directly tells guilty people to eat and enjoy briefly, making enjoyment a temporary rather than approving allowance.
Its command to give from provision is a constructive response to divine bounty, but only indirectly related to the focus.
It links disbelief with the promised day of woe, supporting the focus's certainty of later reckoning.
Its assurance that every report reaches its settled fulfillment explains the force of "you will know."
Its parable of refusing equal partners in one's own provision gives a closely related rational argument against associating partners with God.
Turning away and disbelieving is a broad parallel without the focus's gift-and-reprieve structure.
The promise that opponents will see provides a limited verbal parallel to the focus's future knowledge.
Spending from God's provision is a grateful practice that only indirectly contrasts with denying the giver.
The creation and resurrection signs do not specifically clarify the focus's warning.
Its emphatic future knowledge warning reinforces the focus's declaration that present conduct will be disclosed.
The disconnected letters do not provide interpretive value for the focus.
It states that the enjoyment people had been given will not benefit them when the consequence arrives.
The repeated future-knowledge warning intensifies the focus's threat of eventual disclosure.
Rain reviving the earth does not clarify the focus's themes.
It criticizes those whose knowledge stops at worldly life, directly complementing the focus's contrast between present enjoyment and future knowledge.
The killing of the she-camel does not illuminate the focus.
The opening report of Roman defeat does not clarify the focus.
Its repeated warning that deniers will soon know parallels the focus's deferred disclosure.
The command to watch while opponents will see is a limited verbal parallel to the focus.
The rebuke for failing to reflect on the Quran does not specifically clarify the focus.
Their continued denial is only a broad parallel to the focus's unbelief.
God's comprehensive knowledge for judgment does not add a specific connection to the focus.
The prediction of Roman victory does not clarify the focus.
The angels' reassurance and announcement of a knowledgeable son do not clarify the focus.
It shows a contrasting, merciful form of enjoyment granted to believers until an appointed time.
It labels worldly possessions and desires as enjoyment of this life and contrasts them with the better final return.
Each soul's coming knowledge of what it brought supplies a closely related picture of final disclosure.
It warns that those who deny and mock will receive the news of what they mocked, paralleling the focus's future knowledge.
The certain fulfillment of God's promise, despite most people's ignorance, supports the certainty behind the focus's warning.
Continued denial is only a general parallel to the focus's unbelief.
It shows that even greater granted resources did not protect earlier deniers from God's repudiation.
The register of the righteous does not clarify the focus.
Disbelief in God's signs is a broad parallel, without the focus's response to received gifts.
Pharaoh's threat ending in "you will know" shares the formula but has a different subject and context.
Creation and return to God do not directly clarify the focus's warning about present enjoyment.
It explicitly condemns disbelieving in the Creator while making rivals for Him, closely supporting the focus's anti-association setting.
It warns deniers that the news of what they mocked will come to them, paralleling the focus's future disclosure.
Mockery of believers does not clarify the focus.
Seeking God's protection from satanic provocation does not illuminate the focus.
The absence of a revealed authority for their position loosely supports the surrounding challenge to associators.
The nearby call to glorify God is a broad opposite response to the focus's ingratitude.
God's knowledge of hidden things and deeds does not specifically clarify the focus.
Signs granted as a manifest test loosely parallel the focus's concern with how divine gifts are received.
It explicitly denies that anyone shares God's judgment and grounds that exclusivity in His complete knowledge.
It condemns disbelieving in what God sends down out of envy and links such denial to punishment.
It explicitly describes a little temporary enjoyment before people are driven to severe punishment.
Lot's people invoking their ban on outsiders does not clarify the focus.
God's universal ownership and self-sufficiency explain why unbelief cannot diminish Him and why His gifts must not be misattributed.
The slander against Mary does not clarify the focus.
It characterizes worldly life as deceptive enjoyment that withers and is followed by the decisive hereafter.
It rejects attributing a child to God through His self-sufficiency, universal ownership, and the lack of any authority for the claim.
It explicitly forbids obeying even parents in associating partners with God without knowledge and directs all back to divine accounting.
It commands remembrance and gratitude to God and forbids denying Him, the direct opposite of the focus's response to gifts.
It commands believers to eat from God's provision and thank Him, providing the grateful alternative to the focus's ingratitude.
It explicitly contrasts punishment with gratitude and faith, clarifying the moral significance of the focus's disbelief.
People call on God alone for rescue from land and sea distress and promise gratitude if He saves them.
It immediately states that God alone delivers them from distress, yet they still associate partners with Him.
It recalls humanity's establishment and provision on earth, followed by the rebuke that people give little thanks.
After God grants a sound child, the parents make partners concerning what He gave them, directly matching the focus's pattern.
It rejects the partners made concerning God's gift and declares Him exalted above their association.
In peril at sea people call on God sincerely, but after He saves them they return to wrongdoing.
It makes their post-rescue wrongdoing fall upon themselves and returns them to God for disclosure of their deeds.
It asks who provides from heaven and earth and directs life and death, then identifies God alone as the answer.
It describes human despair when mercy is withdrawn, a limited counterpart to the focus's response after receiving mercy.
After adversity is lifted, people boast that evil has gone, a close parallel to treating relief as self-owned.
It directly contrasts gratitude with the severe consequence of ingratitude.
It attributes rain, fruits, ships, rivers, sun, moon, night, and day to God's provision and ordering.
It states that God gave people what they asked and that human beings are deeply unjust and ungrateful for His favors.
It states without qualification that every blessing people possess is from God.
After God removes distress, a group immediately associate partners with their Lord, forming the direct lead-in to the focus's exact parallel.
It combines unequal provision with the rebuke that people deny God's favor, closely supporting the focus's source-and-denial logic.
It attributes family and good provision to God, then condemns belief in falsehood and denial of His favor.
It condemns worshipping beings unable to provide anything while people deny God's favor.
It says people recognize God's favor and then deny it; most of them are unbelievers.
A town given security and abundant provision becomes ungrateful for God's favors and suffers the resulting deprivation.
In danger at sea people call on God alone, but after rescue they turn away in ingratitude.
It identifies hearing, sight, and hearts as divine gifts and rebukes people's scant gratitude.
It elicits the admission that the earth and all within it belong to God, grounding the focus's rejection of association.
It elicits the admission that all dominion and protection belong to God alone, then rebukes people for being deluded.
It says God distributes water so people may remember, but most insist on disbelief instead.
Solomon treats the gift placed before him as a test of whether he will be grateful or ungrateful.
It asks who begins creation, repeats it, and provides from heaven and earth, then rejects any deity alongside God.
It explicitly says the Lord is bountiful to people, though most of them are not grateful.
People pray to God sincerely in danger at sea, then associate partners with Him after He brings them safely to land.
It diagnoses the associators as following desires without knowledge, immediately preparing the focus's critique of their conduct.
It contrasts self-serving gain with almsgiving that seeks God's face, a limited corrective to treating bounty as self-owned.
It calls people to inspect the end of earlier associators, extending the focus's warning of eventual consequence.
It states that disbelief is borne by its own doer, while righteous action prepares for the final outcome.
It recalls God's manifest and hidden favors and condemns disputing about Him without knowledge or guidance.
After rescue from overwhelming waves, some remain faithful while others prove ungrateful, directly testing the response to salvation.
The people of Saba are told to eat from their Lord's provision and thank Him, the grateful alternative to the focus.
After the people of Saba turn away from their abundant provision, their garden is replaced with a ruinous harvest.
It explicitly identifies this reversal as recompense for their disbelief and asks whether any but the ungrateful are so repaid.
It asks whether any creator besides God provides from heaven and earth, directly denying a basis for associating partners.
It challenges alleged partners to show what they created or what share of creation or authority they possess.
It says people eat from fruits God produced rather than their own handiwork and asks why they do not give thanks.
It obtains the admission that God created the heavens and earth, then exposes the powerlessness of invoked beings besides Him.
After receiving favor following harm, a person claims it was given through personal knowledge, directly exemplifying misattribution of divine bounty.
It states that God expands and restricts provision as He wills, restoring attribution of provision to Him.
It describes God's ordering of night and day and His bounty to people, then notes that most do not give thanks.
After mercy follows harm, a person claims it as his own and denies the coming Hour, closely paralleling the focus's misuse of favor.
It shows people rejoicing when mercy reaches them yet despairing when harm follows their own deeds, extending the focus's diagnosis of their response.
When asked who created the heavens and earth, people admit it was the Mighty, Knowing God.
When asked who created them, people answer God, yet still turn away from the implication.
It demands that alleged partners show what they created or produce a prior authority for their claims.
It recalls that God could make the water people drink bitter and asks why they do not give thanks.
It calls people to eat from the earth's provision while remembering that final return is to God.
It asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, directly denying independent sources of sustenance.
It exposes the mistaken assumption that abundant provision proves personal honor rather than serving as a divine test.
It exposes the corresponding mistake of treating restricted provision as humiliation rather than a divine test.
It directly declares the human being deeply ungrateful to his Lord.
